arguments.title: More money for criminal investigations strengthens protection against poisoned pills sold as real medicine.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 More money for criminal investigations strengthens protection against poisoned pills sold as real medicine.

  • Because Section 102 pays for Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the criminal investigation branch of ICE: “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” [1].
  • Because HSI and its partners have investigated fake pharmacies selling pills made in U.S. drug factories. Their report describes taking pills from those factories: “Law enforcement raided at least three of these pill mills and two other narcotics storage locations, seizing approximately 625,000 counterfeit pills” [6].
  • Because This fraud reaches people seeking health care. The report describes victims “who were in need of medication — people suffering with legitimate ailments.” [6] It reports, “At least nine of the victims later died of narcotics poisoning.” [6]
  • So Added money supports finding these sellers and removing their poisoned pills from sale. That protects people seeking medicine, which gives [NAME] a health reason to favor this added capacity.
arguments.con_html:
Response This argument does not connect its pharmacy case to work that Section 102's limited money may pay for.

  • Because The money must support “functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.” [1] Not every activity of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) is an allowed use of this money. Customs concerns goods crossing the border.
  • Because The case concerns an international drug operation: “Lopez Reyes led the enterprise, orchestrating and controlling every facet of the scheme from the Dominican Republic.” [6] The report also says “the defendants shipped counterfeit pharmaceuticals to victims across the United States and around the world” [6].
  • So Finding pill factories in U.S. basements does not place the investigation outside customs work. This argument names no part of this international case that the limited money would expand outside the excluded missions.

arguments.title: More ability to hold and remove people with violent convictions limits their chances for more attacks.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 More ability to hold and remove people with violent convictions limits their chances for more attacks.

  • Because Section 202 pays for enforcement staff and “transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [1] “Removal” means deportation.
  • Because This work includes custody after a criminal sentence ends. ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) reported that it “apprehended an illegally present Dominican national convicted for murder in Massachusetts in 2007 when officers arrested Cesar Augusto Polanco, 59, January 24 at the Massachusetts Correctional Institution in Norfolk after he was released from state custody.” [7]
  • Because ICE kept him in custody for the removal process: “Polanco remains in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.” [7]
  • So Holding people with violent convictions after prison, and removing them, keeps them away from people they could attack here. Added money for staff and transport supports this protection for U.S. residents such as [NAME].
arguments.con_html:
Response One detention does not show that S.2's broader removal money reduces residents' exposure to violence.

  • Because Research on a similar detention and deportation program found, “The results show that the Secure Communities program has had no observable effect on the overall crime rate.” [9] Secure Communities shared local arrest fingerprints with immigration officials.
  • Because A separate study of violent victimization (being a victim of violent crime) in 2005–2014 reports, “The activation of 287(g) jail enforcement agreements and anti-detainer policies had no significant impact on violent victimization risk during the period.” [10]
  • So The example shows one person kept apart from the public. These studies weigh against assuming that more of this enforcement means less violence. They cover older programs and wider crime measures, so they do not settle what would happen with people who have violent convictions.

arguments.title: Supporting transfers from jails makes safer arrests possible.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 Supporting transfers from jails makes safer arrests possible.

  • Because Section 202 pays for partnerships with state and local police: “Supporting coordination with state and local authorities by expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act” [1].
  • Because One kind of agreement lets trained local officers identify people in jail for immigration proceedings. ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) explains that they “place them into immigration proceedings at the time of release from state or local custody.” [11]
  • Because A transfer can avoid a dangerous arrest in public. In the Polanco case, ICE said cooperation let officers “make the arrest in the safety of a jail cell rather than sending a team of officers into the community to make a potentially dangerous arrest.” [7]
  • So Paying for these partnerships supports more arrests in controlled places. Keeping these confrontations out of public places protects people nearby, which gives [NAME] a separate reason based on personal safety.
arguments.con_html:
Response Expanding 287(g) agreements does not show that jail transfers would replace public arrests.

  • Because These agreements give local officers some immigration powers outside jails too. ICE's February 2026 description says, “The Task Force Model allows your officers to enforce limited immigration authority while performing routine police duties or as an active participant in an ICE-led task force.” [12]
  • Because Section 202 pays for agreements in general. It also pays for “release monitoring, transportation, and arrests of covered unlawful aliens encountered in jurisdictions that are not qualified cooperating jurisdictions” [1].
  • So More authority to make immigration arrests is different from moving the same arrests into jails. This example shows that one transfer was safe. It does not show a change in where arrests happen because of S.2.

Point 5 Paying for trafficking investigations strengthens protection against forced work and sexual violence.

  • Because Section 102 pays for staff of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI, the part of ICE that investigates crimes), including “other necessary expenses for Homeland Security Investigations' mission support and operations and maintenance” [1]. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) says HSI “conducts criminal human trafficking investigations worldwide.” [13] Human trafficking means forcing or tricking people into work or sex.

  • Because Traffickers' control includes “actual physical assaults and sexual violence” [13]. Finding victims also opens a way to help, including “medical and mental health care, safety planning, and legal services” [13].
  • So Added money supports finding violent exploitation and bringing victims into protection and care. Protection against abuse through everyday work and relationships serves the personal safety [NAME] values.

arguments.title: Paying for border checks strengthens screening for terrorism threats before entry or release.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 7 Paying for border checks strengthens screening for terrorism threats before entry or release.

  • Because Section 201 pays for border agents and support staff “in order to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1]
  • Because The Border Patrol uses names, photographs and fingerprints in these checks. Its inspector general (an internal auditor) reports: “The e3 Portal captures biographical information, photos, and fingerprints and automatically compares them to a series of Federal law enforcement databases that provide real-time potential criminal history information, including wants, warrant data, and terrorist watchlist matches.” [17]
  • Because The checks inform decisions to release people: “We determined that Border Patrol agents conducted required record checks and verified the checks did not contain derogatory information before releasing the migrants from our sample.” [17]
  • So Paying and equipping agents supports a check for security threats before people enter U.S. communities. That protection against terrorism serves [NAME]'s wish to avoid danger.
arguments.con_html:
Response The reported end of releases narrows this argument's example about screening before release.

  • Because The inspector general found that agents finished record checks before releasing migrants in its sample. That 2022 audit describes how the check worked then. [17]
  • Because A June 9 congressional press release says Customs and Border Protection (CBP) had announced in May “a full year of zero releases at the border.” [18] This is one account, not a separately checked measure of every encounter or way into the country.
  • So The older release audit does not show how much checks before release matter under the policy reported at the comparison date. This response is partial. It does not answer the case for keeping checks at the first encounter or before entry, and it does not show that added staff cannot support those checks.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence note: A June 9 congressional press release says Customs and Border Protection (CBP) had reported a full year of zero releases at the border. This press release concerns screening before release more directly than screening when agents first encounter people or before entry. These sources do not separately confirm all release or entry practices. They also do not show that keeping the screening system has no value. Sources: [18], [17].

arguments.title: Supporting existing border health duties strengthens protection against infectious disease.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 8 Supporting existing border health duties strengthens protection against infectious disease.

  • Because Section 101 pays for Border Patrol staff for “functions other than immigration enforcement and customs functions.” [1]
  • Because The Border Patrol had an “immediate requirement to assist the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in implementing its May 18, 2026 Order” [19], with guidance on “screening, processing, and expulsion procedures under Title 42 authority.” [19] These are duties under public health law.
  • Because The May 18 order's stated term covered June 9: “This order will be in effect for 30 days, effective immediately.” [20] The CDC described its goal as “preventing its introduction into the United States.” [20] It explains the danger: “Ebola is a serious viral disease that spreads through direct contact with infected bodily fluids and can be fatal.” [21]
  • Because The CDC issued a continuing order on June 21, effective at 5:00 p.m. that day through July 21, and asked the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to help enforce it. This later evidence shows that DHS's supporting role continued after the May order's stated term. It does not name the Border Patrol, show unbroken coverage between the orders, or settle whether Section 101 can pay for this work. [22]
  • So Paying staff who carry out these existing health protections supports efforts to keep infection from reaching U.S. communities while the health orders apply. [NAME]'s wish to avoid disease gives a reason to support this added help.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html: Evidence limitation: A May account from Customs and Border Protection (CBP) gives the Border Patrol a supporting role under Title 42, a public health law. The June order from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) asks the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for help. It names customs officers and the Coast Guard. The June CDC order does not say how spending under Section 101 should be classified. One question stays open. Would Border Patrol help with the public health orders be allowed under Section 101, be excluded as immigration or customs work, or qualify under another part of the bill? Sources: [1], [19], [22].

arguments.title: More enforcement operations expose people going about daily life to violence by agents.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 More enforcement operations expose people going about daily life to violence by agents.

  • Because Section 202 pays for more enforcement staff: “Hiring, paying, training, and equipping U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement personnel and the personnel for all its directorates, including officers, agents, investigators, attorneys and support staff, to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1]
  • Because Citizens have been physically harmed: “Americans have been dragged, tackled, beaten, tased and shot by immigration agents.” [25]
  • Because People can be caught up while doing ordinary things. ProPublica reports that “agents grabbed and handcuffed a woman on her way to work who was caught up in a chaotic raid on street vendors.” [25]
  • So More operations using these practices create more chances for dangerous encounters during work and travel. [NAME]'s wish to avoid injury or death gives a reason to oppose this added exposure.
arguments.con_html:
Response This argument assumes that added enforcement would repeat the street practices behind its injury reports, despite a change in enforcement before June 9.

  • Because ProPublica links rising citizen detentions to a particular approach: “large-scale immigration sweeps across the country, often in communities that do not want them.” [25]
  • Because On May 1, the Associated Press reported a shift “away from aggressive, public-facing tactics toward a quieter approach to enforcement.” [26] It also reported that “there have been no new high-profile city-based operations launched” [26].
  • So The 2025 list of incidents does not show how S.2 changes dangerous encounters under the later approach. The missing step is why added operations would spread the practices that caused those injuries. This does not show that such practices have ended.

arguments.title: Expanding local police immigration work weakens the crime reporting that protects the public.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 Expanding local police immigration work weakens the crime reporting that protects the public.

  • Because S.2 pays for 287(g) agreements, which let local police do immigration enforcement: “Supporting coordination with state and local authorities by expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1357(g)).” [1]
  • Because The program again includes a street-policing version, called the task force model: “Allows officers trained by ICE to enforce immigration law during routine police activity, like traffic stops.” [29]
  • Because A study using national crime-victim survey data from 2005–2014 found a higher risk of being a victim of violent crime: “the activation of Secure Communities and 287(g) task force agreements significantly increased violent victimization risk among Latinos” [10].
  • Because The reporting problem also weakens police protection for the wider public. The president of the Major Cities Chiefs Association explained: “Whether we seek to stop child predators, drug dealers, rapists or robbers – we need the full cooperation of victims and witness. Cooperation is not forthcoming from persons who see their police as immigration agents.” [30]
  • Because A February–March 2026 survey with a random sample of adults in Minneapolis and St. Paul asked about Operation Metro Surge, a large federal immigration deployment. In Minneapolis 49.4% and in St. Paul 46.1% agreed that they were less likely to seek help from police because of how ICE and Border Patrol agents carried it out. These are reported intentions about a federal operation, not measured crime results or an effect of local police working under 287(g). [31]
  • So Paying to expand this police role expands a barrier to reporting crime and helping investigations. [NAME] relies on police being able to find and stop dangerous offenders, so this loss of cooperation gives [NAME] a personal safety reason to oppose S.2.
arguments.con_html:
Response The evidence supports a concern about people seeking help, but it does not show which added local agreements cause a wider loss of protection.

  • Because S.2 pays for local police immigration work through “expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g)” [1], without choosing between street policing and checks inside jails.
  • Because The older study reports that “our results for 287(g) jail programs showed no significant association with violent victimization risk” [10]. Its results for street policing and Secure Communities showed “no evident impact on victimization risk among non-Latino Whites and Blacks.” [10]
  • Because The study cannot separate reduced trust from other explanations: “The data assembled for our study cannot discern between these potential explanations.” [10] The newer Twin Cities survey reports less willingness to seek police help among adult residents. But it concerns federal agents' conduct during a large surge, ended in March, and does not isolate local police, 287(g) or actual reporting. [31]
  • So These limits narrow the step from older victimization results and reported intentions to added local agreements. They do not answer the concern about seeking help, and they do not show that only Latinos could be affected.

These are reported intentions about a federal operation, not measured crime outcomes or an effect of local police working under 287(g). [31]
  • So Paying to expand this police role expands a barrier to reporting crime and helping investigations. [NAME] relies on police being able to identify and stop dangerous offenders, so this loss of cooperation gives [NAME] a personal safety reason to oppose S.2.
original.con_html:
Response The evidence supports a help-seeking concern but does not identify which added local agreements cause a wider loss of protection.

  • Because S.2 funds local police immigration work through “expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g)” [1], without choosing between street policing and checks inside jails.
  • Because The older study reports that “our results for 287(g) jail programs showed no significant association with violent victimization risk” [10]. Its street-policing and Secure Communities results showed “no evident impact on victimization risk among non-Latino Whites and Blacks.” [10]
  • Because The study cannot distinguish reduced trust from other explanations: “The data assembled for our study cannot discern between these potential explanations.” [10] The newer Twin Cities survey reports reduced willingness to seek police help across adult residents, but it concerns federal agents' conduct during a large surge, ended fieldwork in March, and does not isolate local police, 287(g) or actual reporting. [31]

arguments.title: Expanded enforcement gives violent criminals more cover to pretend to be immigration agents.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 Expanded enforcement gives violent criminals more cover to pretend to be immigration agents.

  • Because The FBI has documented the danger: “Criminals posing as US immigration officers have carried out robberies, kidnappings, and sexual assaults in several states” [32].
  • Because Its bulletin connects this danger to how visible enforcement has become. WIRED reports that “criminals are using Immigration and Custom Enforcement’s heightened profile to target vulnerable communities, making it harder for Americans to distinguish between lawful officers and imposters while eroding trust in law enforcement.” [32]
  • Because S.2 leaves masked operations in place: “The GOP bill does not restrict mask-wearing” [33] GOP means the Republican Party..
  • So More operations in this form give fake officers more of the cover (conditions that help them hide) they already use and make fake arrests harder to recognize. Avoiding robbery, kidnapping and assault gives [NAME] a safety reason to oppose this expansion.
arguments.con_html:
Response The FBI's warning rests partly on public visibility, which had reportedly fallen before S.2, and the mask point marks no change.

  • Because WIRED reports that criminals use ICE's “heightened profile to target vulnerable communities, making it harder for Americans to distinguish between lawful officers and imposters while eroding trust in law enforcement.” [32] The same report links the rise in these crimes to the “recent increase in ICE enforcement actions” [32].
  • Because Before S.2, the Associated Press reported a move toward “a quieter approach to enforcement.” [26] It also reported that “ICE arrests have fallen in recent months” [26]. More enforcement work and a higher public profile are different changes.
  • Because The mask point is a reform that was not made: “The GOP bill does not restrict mask-wearing” [33]. It does not introduce the practice.
  • So A public profile from the earlier period may not carry over to quieter operations, and keeping an existing mask practice does not itself create extra cover. This narrows the argument to the link between enforcement actions and pretending to be officers. It does not show that added operations would create no more cover.

arguments.title: More enforcement and removals threaten the supply of care when Americans need it.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 5 More enforcement and removals threaten the supply of care when Americans need it.

  • Because S.2 pays for deportations: “Funding for transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [1]
  • Because Past enforcement reduced nursing care. A study comparing counties as Secure Communities began found that “the program reduced directcare staff hours per resident day” [34]. These are hours of hands-on care in nursing homes. Secure Communities shared local arrest fingerprints with immigration officials.
  • Because Another study of that program's start in 2008–2013 found both fewer home care workers and less help for older adults: “We find that Secure Communities reduces the overall size of the home care workforce by 7.5%” [35]; “older adults needing assistance are 2.9 percentage points less likely to receive any help at home” [35].
  • Because Among Twin Cities survey respondents who missed work over enforcement concerns, about 28% reported a caregiver who could not come. This is a local self-report about disrupted care, not a drop in the national care workforce. [31]
  • So S.2 pays to expand local immigration checks, arrests and removals. The earlier program and recent reports support a risk to care being available. They do not estimate how much S.2 would add to this risk.
  • Because Long-term care is an ordinary health need over a lifetime: “Most Americans will need long-term care at some point in their lifetimes” [35].
  • Because Shortages also threaten hospital care. JAMA, a medical journal, explains: “The resulting shortages could reverberate through emergency departments and hospitals, leading to the inability to discharge patients and tying up nurses and other staff.” [36]
  • So [NAME] depends on timely care, whether at home, in a nursing home or in a hospital. Protecting access to this care gives [NAME] a health reason to oppose the added enforcement money.

arguments.pro_html:
Point 6 More enforcement around health care makes it harder to find and treat disease in the community.

  • Because Enforcement already reaches medical settings: “The Infectious Diseases Society of America is alarmed by reports of immigration enforcement activity occurring near health care settings.” [38]

arguments.title: Supporting more detention keeps a route open for infections to reach the wider public.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 7 Supporting more detention keeps a route open for infections to reach the wider public.

  • Because S.2 pays to keep enforcement facilities running: “Funding for facility maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations.” [1]
  • Because KFF, a health research group, reports “recent measles outbreaks in Arizona and Texas detention facilities” [28] and explains: “Overcrowding as well as limited capacity and resources may also increase the risk of the spread of communicable diseases, such as measles.” [28] Communicable diseases are diseases that spread between people.
  • Because Outbreaks have infected people outside the detained population. In its report on mumps outbreaks in 2018–2019 in migrant detention facilities, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recorded that “an additional 33 cases occurred among staff members.” [41]
  • Because Staff connect detention facilities to daily community life: “ICE detention facilities are often located in small, isolated towns that employ local residents who move each day between facility and community.” [42]
  • So More arrests feeding this system, and money to keep it running, increase chances for infections to reach the public through staff. [NAME]'s interest in avoiding disease gives a reason to oppose this added exposure.
arguments.con_html:
Response The sources limit the step from more detention to more infection through crowding.

  • Because KFF's warning about crowding has a condition: detention “can lead to overcrowding if deportations do not keep up with the pace of arrests” [28]. S.2 pays for facility upkeep and also for “transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [1]
  • Because The CDC's 2019 report records “an additional 33 cases occurred among staff members.” [41] It also records a real response: “IHSC provided >25,000 doses of measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine in response to mumps in 56 facilities.” [41] IHSC is ICE's health service.
  • So More arrests do not by themselves show more crowding when the bill also pays for departures and upkeep, and vaccination can limit outbreaks. This response is partial. It does not deny the route through staff who travel between the facility and the community.

  • Because KFF's crowding warning depends on the balance between arrivals and departures: detention “can lead to overcrowding if deportations do not keep up with the pace of arrests” [28]. S.2 funds both facility upkeep and “transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [1]

arguments.title: More enforcement spreads fear and mental health harm beyond the people detained.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 8 More enforcement spreads fear and mental health harm beyond the people detained.

  • Because Psychiatrists describe the link from enforcement fears to illness: “Fear of detention, deportation, or family separation acts as a chronic psychological stressor, contributing to anxiety, depression, trauma-related symptoms, sleep disturbance, isolation from community support, and worsening of serious mental illness.” [40] A stressor is something that causes long-term strain.
  • Because People do not need to be detained to suffer these effects: “Reports of violent encounters involving federal immigration agents, including recent fatal and non fatal shootings, intensify fear, psychological distress, and community-wide trauma.” [40]
  • So Paying for more of these operations exposes the wider community to fear and trauma. [NAME]'s wish to protect mental health and be personally secure gives a reason to oppose this expansion.
arguments.con_html:
Response This argument extends distress in communities facing enforcement to [NAME] without showing the exposure that it needs.

  • Because The psychiatric statement names the stressor as “Fear of detention, deportation, or family separation” [40]. It also says reports of violent encounters “intensify fear, psychological distress, and community-wide trauma.” [40]
  • Because It extends the harm beyond patients to families and affected communities: “These harms extend beyond individual patients to families and communities, with children particularly vulnerable to the destabilizing effects of fear, uncertainty, and parental separation.” [40]
  • So Exposure can come through reports as well as direct encounters. But the argument still must connect S.2's added enforcement to fear or illness for [NAME], read here as an average American. Being outside detention does not establish that connection. Calling trauma “community-wide” does not fill this gap.

arguments.title: S.2 gives security agencies steadier money to keep trained officers ready.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 S.2 gives security agencies steadier money to keep trained officers ready.

  • Because The April 2026 yearly funding law left out the Border Patrol and ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement): it “did not include funding for the U.S. Border Patrol or U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement” [2].
  • Because An April 3 presidential directive had already told the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to use funds with “a reasonable and logical nexus to the functions of DHS” to pay employees during this gap, “subject to the availability of appropriations.” A nexus is a link. So S.2 adds money set aside for these agencies on top of this instruction. It does not create the first possible way to pay them. [3]
  • Because S.2 adds money available through September 2029 “to hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and Border Patrol support personnel” [1]. It also adds flexible money that the administration describes as “$5 billion in additional appropriations to DHS to account for any unforeseen costs that ICE and Border Patrol may incur in future years” [4].
  • So Money that lasts across budget years, pays officers and covers unexpected costs supports a ready security workforce. That serves [NAME]'s concern for a strong state able to defend people.

Staff for the minority party on the Senate Budget Committee reported money not yet committed to spending (unobligated) at the end of May: $62 billion for ICE and $33 billion for CBP. The April 3 presidential directive told the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to pay employees from funds with a link (nexus) to its functions, subject to law and available money from Congress (appropriations). These sources contain no audit of pay for individual employees. The Government Accountability Office (GAO), a federal audit agency, reported that Border Patrol agents were leaving faster than new agents were hired, and that a large wave of retirements was coming. The case that S.2 gives steadier money is weakest for ICE. The sources do not settle how much S.2 would add. Sources: [1], [5], [2], [4], [3], [6], [7], [8].

arguments.title: S.2 strengthens control over land and sea borders.
arguments.pro_html:

arguments.title: S.2 makes identity and departure checks harder to avoid.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 S.2 makes identity and departure checks harder to avoid.

  • Because S.2 pays for identity checks based on physical traits, such as face images: “Necessary expenses, including the deployment of technology, relating to the biometric entry and exit system” [1]. “Biometric” means based on the body, such as a face or fingerprint.
  • Because Customs and Border Protection (CBP) explains that its face-comparison service can “identify the traveler biometrically and to enable CBP to confirm and expedite the traveler’s arrival or departure.” [12]
  • Because CBP reports that “facial comparison results in better security by reducing imposter threats.” [12] It also uses departure checks for security: “CBP performs watchlist vetting of departing travelers.” [12] A watchlist is a government list of people of security concern.
  • So More reliable identity and departure checks make false identities harder to use and strengthen checks against security records. This supports the state's ability to control who crosses its borders and to find threats.
arguments.con_html:
Response Documented limits weaken the step from this money to wider or better identity checks.

  • Because The Customs and Border Protection (CBP) report from March 2025 already said it “has the capacity to support increased usage of CBP biometric matching service as more airlines participate.” [12]
  • Because Growth in checks at airports for departing passengers also depends on airlines and airports choosing to join. CBP's requirements say participation “is voluntary and is not mandated by CBP.” [14]
  • So So capacity of the matching service and money may not be what limits coverage at airports. This does not show that the money could not help in other ways, because Section 103 also pays for “the deployment of technology” [1].

arguments.title: S.2 strengthens defenses against fentanyl and other dangerous drugs.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 S.2 strengthens defenses against fentanyl and other dangerous drugs.

  • Because S.2 pays for inspection equipment “to combat the entry or exit of illicit narcotics at ports of entry and along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders.” [1] Its purposes include fighting “fentanyl and its precursor chemicals” [1], the chemicals used to make it.
  • Because This equipment has stopped drugs. For fiscal year 2023, Customs and Border Protection (CBP) reported that large-scale scanning systems were “aiding in the interdiction of more than 127,000 pounds of narcotics” [10]. Interdiction means stopping and seizing.
  • Because CBP explains the protective step: “Seizures remove dangerous drugs from illicit supply chains, keep them out of our communities, and deny TCOs valuable profits.” [10] TCOs are criminal groups that work across countries.
  • So More ways to detect and stop drugs strengthen protection against a deadly threat to U.S. communities, which gives [NAME] a security reason to favor the bill.
arguments.con_html:
Response The past seizure total does not show that S.2 would turn equipment purchases into more effective drug inspections.

  • Because S.2 pays for inspection equipment and “associated civil works” [1], meaning work to prepare sites. Other steps include good deployment plans, trained operators and reliable repairs.
  • Because The inspector general of the Department of Homeland Security found that CBP “did not follow Department of Homeland Security acquisition policy, did not consider relevant information during planning, and did not have a well-defined maintenance and sustainment plan” [15]. These findings concerned purchases and operations before S.2.
  • Because The Government Accountability Office's January 2026 testimony reported that officials at all four field offices it visited “did not always have sufficient staff to fully use the systems.” [16]
  • So This argument does not connect the added spending to usable inspections under those conditions. The amount of drugs seized by earlier systems does not supply this connection.

arguments.title: S.2 strengthens arrest and removal operations against people who threaten public safety.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 5 S.2 strengthens arrest and removal operations against people who threaten public safety.

  • Because S.2 pays for ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) staff and “transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” [1] “Removal” means deportation.
  • Because S.2 sets aside “Not less than $350,000,000” [1] for work including “custodial transfer, release monitoring, transportation, and arrests of covered unlawful aliens encountered in jurisdictions that are not qualified cooperating jurisdictions” [1].
  • Because S.2 also pays for local cooperation: “Supporting coordination with state and local authorities by expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g)” [1]. Under the jail version of these agreements, local officers help “identify criminal aliens and immigration violators in state and local custody and place them into immigration proceedings at the time of release from state or local custody.” [17]
  • Because These tools reach people with serious criminal records. ICE's 2024 arrests included charges and convictions for “sexual assault and sex offenses” [18] and “homicides” [18]. ICE explains the custody link: “When criminal noncitizens complete their sentences, ICE assumes custody and places them in the appropriate removal proceedings.” [18]
  • So More staff, custody transfers and transport give ICE more ways to keep removable violent offenders from returning to communities after prison and to carry out their removal. That strengthens public protection, which [NAME] values.
arguments.con_html:
Response This argument does not establish that the broader arrest and removal money would add protection from violent offenders.

  • Because The $350 million provision covers people after “an arrest, charge, booking, or conviction for a criminal offense under Federal, State, or local law, other than a minor traffic offense” [1]. A violent conviction is not required.
  • Because A federally funded study using 2005–2010 data on places that applied for 287(g) agreements concluded: “We find no evidence that these 287(g) arrangements had meaningful crime reduction benefits.” [19]
  • So Serious crimes among earlier ICE arrests do not show the effect of expanding these broader operations. The study weighs against assuming that more immigration enforcement means less violence. It covers an older period and wider crime measures, so it does not settle what would happen with people who have violent convictions.

arguments.title: S.2 strengthens criminal cases against terrorists and violent gangs.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 6 S.2 strengthens criminal cases against terrorists and violent gangs.

  • Because Section 102 pays “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” [1]. Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) is the part of ICE that investigates crimes.
  • Because HSI builds criminal cases against “terrorist networks and facilitators” [20], including the people who help those networks operate.
  • Because HSI also pursues violent gangs. Its 2024 report describes gang cases involving “firearms trafficking and possession, violent crimes, terroristic acts” [18] and reports that gang investigations produced “2,189 indictments and 1,106 convictions.” [18]
  • So Paying investigators who build these cases strengthens the state's ability to stop organized violence and terrorism. That directly serves [NAME]'s concern that the United States defend itself against threats.
arguments.con_html:
Response Past terrorism and gang cases by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) do not show that S.2 would put more investigators on these cases.

  • Because A January 2026 Senate letter reported that agents had been taken off criminal cases. It said a joint FBI-HSI investigation into suspected terrorist financing through Iranian oil shipments “has suffered from the redeployment” [21].
  • So Historical cases do not show the claimed change in investigators available for this work under the later reported practice of moving agents to immigration work. This does not show that added money could not reach it.

Shared objection Reported changes in staff assignments weaken the step from a larger general budget for Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) to more staff for the work in this argument.

  • Because In January 2026, senators reported that “entire HSI units have reportedly been reassigned” [21] to immigration enforcement. This is not a finding about where Section 102 hires would work in the future.
  • Because Section 102’s limit governs “funds provided in this section” [1]. Section 202 separately pays staff across “all its directorates” [1] “to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1]
  • So Section 102 limits how its own money may be used. It does not decide how staff paid from other money will be assigned. The reports of reassignment give a reason to question whether added capacity reaches this work. They do not show that added capacity cannot reach it, or that Section 102 hires would be reassigned.

Response Ten years of seizures do not show that S.2 would add to the financial investigations that produced them.

arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 S.2 pays for more street operations with a record of harming the people the state should protect.

  • Because Human Rights Watch documented immigration agents “detaining people based on their perceived race, ethnicity, or national origin, and using excessive force.” [27]
  • Because The harm reaches citizens. The Brennan Center, a law and policy institute, says Democratic legislators blocked more funding for the Department of Homeland Security and demanded reforms after “the killing of U.S. citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis.” [26]
  • Because Human Rights Watch said on June 16 that Congress approved S.2 “without adopting essential oversight and accountability reforms.” [27] Lawmakers and activists had proposed reforms such as requiring warrants from judges and stronger bans on racial profiling.
  • Because S.2 also gives money outside the yearly funding decisions. The American Action Forum, a policy group, says S.2 “provides funding for federal agencies that are typically funded through the annual appropriations process.” [25]
  • So More operating money through 2029 gives these operations more resources and less need to ask for yearly approval. That weakens a practical way for Congress to demand safer conduct. Paying for more exposure to documented violence undermines the citizen protection [NAME] values.
arguments.con_html:
Response This argument does not link the added money to more use of the street tactics behind its examples.

  • Because Reported practices had changed in some places before Congress's June 9 vote. May reporting from Chicago found: “Community leaders and rapid responders say they are seeing more targeted arrests rather than the large, highly visible sweeps seen last fall.” [28]
  • Because The commander of the Minneapolis operation had also left: “Bovino was relieved of his command following Pretti's killing and retired from Border Patrol in March.” [29]
  • So This argument projects earlier tactics onto the added money without accounting for the reported changes. This response does not answer its point about yearly funding, and it does not show that these tactics have ended.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: Money already in law: The Congressional Research Service (CRS) says the 2025 money for detention and enforcement is available in fiscal years 2025 through 2029. Sources: [5].

Context note: The 2025 budget law provided Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) with $45 billion for detention and $29.85 billion for other functions. A June 9 analysis reports plans to use that money to cover (offset) $416 million in detention costs and $350 million in transport costs in fiscal year 2027. The sources do not settle how much S.2 would add. Sources: [5], [30].

arguments.title: S.2 adds to the heavy enforcement that violent criminals use when they pretend to be officers.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 S.2 adds to the heavy enforcement that violent criminals use when they pretend to be officers.

  • Because S.2 adds no ban on masks. A member of Congress said of S.2 and an earlier funding law: “This bill, just like the last one, does not prohibit any agent from wearing a mask.” [34]
  • Because An FBI bulletin reported real attacks: “Criminals posing as US immigration officers have carried out robberies, kidnappings, and sexual assaults in several states” [35].
  • Because The FBI advisory linked rising impersonation crimes (crimes by people pretending to be officers) to the “recent increase in ICE enforcement actions” [35]. WIRED reports confusion “making it harder for Americans to distinguish between lawful officers and imposters while eroding trust in law enforcement.” [35]
  • So Paying for more operations without addressing this confusion keeps up the chances for criminals to borrow federal authority. That threatens residents' safety and their ability to recognize real protection.
arguments.con_html:
Response The mask and identification rules do not change under S.2, and the public-profile part of the FBI's link rests on 2025 conditions.

  • Because The FBI account ties impersonation to the “recent increase in ICE enforcement actions” [35] and ICE's “heightened profile” [35], citing “five 2025 incidents” [35]. It documents crimes under the existing enforcement campaign, not a change in identification caused by S.2.
  • Because The report separates existing rules from its advice. Officers must identify themselves “as soon as it is practical and safe to do so.” [35] The FBI also recommends that officers “cooperate with individuals who request further verification” [35]. The bill does not change the identification rule.
  • Because May 2026 reports describe less public operations. Chicago-area community leaders reported “more targeted arrests rather than the large, highly visible sweeps seen last fall” [28], and Tom Homan, a top administration official on border policy, said “fewer viral videos of ICE agents making arrests” [29] came from targeted operations. Neither report says that enforcement stopped.
  • So Having no mask ban does not show added confusion compared with existing law, and a 2025 public profile may not fully carry over to less visible operations. This narrows the argument to the link with the number of enforcement actions. It does not show that added operations would create no more opening for impersonators.

arguments.title: S.2 supports assignments that pull investigators away from other serious threats.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 5 S.2 supports assignments that pull investigators away from other serious threats.

  • Because Section 202 pays ICE staff, “including officers, agents, investigators, attorneys and support staff, to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1] ICE is Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
  • Because Section 203 also allows money “for DHS and State officers to carry out immigration enforcement” [2]. DHS means the Department of Homeland Security.
  • Because The campaign has already moved federal investigators: “The Trump administration has already diverted thousands of law enforcement officials at multiple agencies away from their work tackling serious crime and national security investigations to focus on immigration” [36].
  • Because These assignments have real costs for child-abuse investigations: “These delays can mean the difference between building a case against a predator and letting the trail go cold.” [37]
  • Note Section 102's separate investigation money is limited to “functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.” [1] This limit governs that money; Sections 202 and 203 still pay for the immigration assignments above.
  • So S.2 pays for a campaign that uses investigators for deportation work in place of other protective duties. Keeping this diversion leaves serious crimes and national security threats less fully covered, which goes against [NAME]'s concern that the country defend itself against all threats.
arguments.con_html:
Response This argument does not show that S.2 worsens the staff shortage behind the reported diversion of investigators.

  • Because Section 202 pays for “Hiring, paying, training, and equipping” [1] immigration staff. So more immigration work can use new staff. This is not evidence of more transfers from other cases.
  • Because Section 102 adds $7.45 billion for Homeland Security Investigations (HSI): “$7,450,000,000” [1]. Its money “shall be used for functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.” [1]
  • Because Within that amount, “$108,500,000 shall be used to hire, pay, and equip additional child exploitation investigators and forensics analysts” [1]. This pays for additional people for the work that this argument says lacks staff.
  • So The protected investigation money matters to the claimed staff loss, even though other money can pay for immigration assignments. This argument has not shown that the new hiring money leaves a larger staff gap or causes more investigators to leave other protective work.

arguments.title: S.2 pays for tools used to frighten people who peacefully watch the government.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 6 S.2 pays for tools used to frighten people who peacefully watch the government.

  • Because The Brennan Center, a law and policy institute, predicts wider monitoring from the funding it describes, which includes S.2's money: “The funding will also allow DHS to continue to build surveillance capabilities that facilitate indiscriminate collection of information about Americans as well as immigrants.” [26] DHS is the Department of Homeland Security.
  • Because Threats against observers (people who watch and record immigration agents) are documented: “a government lawyer told a federal judge in Maine that agents had violated Department of Homeland Security policy by threatening to put the observers' information into a database.” [38]
  • Because These threats discourage people from watching officers. A lawyer seeking information about ICE's surveillance explained: “If people think that protesting or filming law enforcement may put them in a secret database, many will stay silent” [38].
  • So Paying for more monitoring gives officials tools to frighten people who record their conduct. A state that silences peaceful warnings about its own abuses becomes less answerable for protecting citizens. That threatens safe, stable government.
arguments.con_html:
Response The observer example does not show that S.2 expands the monitoring used to discourage people from watching.

  • Because The quoted lawyer says threats can scare observers “regardless of whether such databases even exist.” [38] The report shows a threat. It does not show the database or technology behind it.
  • Because S.2 pays for technology maintenance for “enforcement and removal operations” [1]. Its additional DHS money is also tied to listed uses: “for the purposes provided in this title or in paragraph (3) or (7) of section 100051 of Public Law 119-21.” [1] These spending permissions do not name an added project to track peaceful observers.
  • So This argument does not connect added monitoring from S.2 to more intimidation or less effective watching. A threat that can work without the claimed database does not supply this link.

arguments.title: S.2 disrupts the everyday work and institutions that keep communities stable.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 7 S.2 disrupts the everyday work and institutions that keep communities stable.

  • Because During the Minneapolis enforcement operation, “Workers stayed home. Small businesses shuttered, and tens of thousands of residents were suddenly thrown into food and housing insecurity.” [34]
  • Because KFF, a health research group, reports that immigrants and family members avoided activities including “going to church or other community activities, going to work, or taking their child to school or school events due to immigration-related fears.” [39]
  • So Fear that keeps people from work, school and community life makes towns less able to function. Paying for more operations with this pattern threatens the social stability [NAME] values.
arguments.con_html:
Response The Minneapolis evidence may not carry over to added operations, and the survey came before the reported change in tactics.

  • Because Before Congress's June 9 vote, the president had ordered the Minneapolis operation wound down (gradually ended). He gave this job to Tom Homan, a top administration official on border policy: “Earlier this year, Mr. Trump charged Homan with winding down the Minneapolis operation” [29]. Independent May reporting also found that Border Patrol groups in Chicago “no longer are making surprise visits to Michigan Avenue or marching through Little Village, Back of the Yards and other neighborhoods.” [28]
  • Because KFF's evidence about avoided activities came from the “KFF/New York Times 2025 Survey of Immigrants (August 28-October 20, 2025).” [39] It measured fears before the changes above.
  • So Continued immigration enforcement does not show continued use of the particular surge tactics, so the Minneapolis disruption is weak evidence about added operations. This does not show that fear has gone down, and the survey still supports a link between enforcement fears and avoided activities.

arguments.title: S.2 supports a detention plan that threatens local water and sewage systems.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 10 S.2 supports a detention plan that threatens local water and sewage systems.

  • Because S.2 pays for “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions.” [1]
  • Because The planned network of ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) includes a large facility in Social Circle, Georgia. The city's February assessment states that “the total additional water demand required for a facility of this scale simply exceeds what the City’s system is capable of providing.” [43]
  • Because Its May 2026 lawsuit warns of “sewer main backups” [44] and “contamination of groundwater and local waterways.” [44]
  • So Money for running the planned detention network supports demands that essential local systems cannot meet. Threats to drinking water and sewage disposal undermine public health and the basic services on which stable communities depend.
arguments.con_html:
Response The Social Circle evidence does not show that S.2 increases the risk to water and sewer systems from that project.

  • Because In March, the city blocked the water connection and explained: “The lock is there until ICE indicates how water and sewer will be served without exceeding our limited infrastructure capacity” [45]. So there was a limit on the project before S.2.
  • Because S.2 pays for “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions.” [1] It does not change the project's water access or review rules.
  • So The warnings concern one project's design and operation. This argument has not shown that S.2 changes how that project gets water or disposes of waste. This limit could change later, and this response does not cover other sites.

arguments.title: S.2's added debt increases pressure on financial stability and readiness for emergencies.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 11 S.2's added debt increases pressure on financial stability and readiness for emergencies.

  • Because The American Action Forum estimates the bill's borrowing cost: “After accounting for roughly $25 billion of additional interest costs, the package would increase budget deficits by $94.5 billion over the FY 2026–2035 budget window.” [25] Here “the package” means S.2, and FY means fiscal year.   • Because The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) explains the general risk: “Larger amounts of debt make the United States’ fiscal position more vulnerable to an increase in interest rates.” [46]

  • So S.2 adds borrowing and interest costs to the money pressures facing future decisions about defense and emergencies. Increasing this burden weakens the financial strength needed for a state that can protect its citizens.

original.title: Its added debt increases pressure on financial stability and readiness for emergencies.
original.pro_html:
Point 11 Its added debt increases pressure on financial stability and readiness for emergencies.

  • Because The American Action Forum estimates the bill's borrowing cost: “After accounting for roughly $25 billion of additional interest costs, the package would increase budget deficits by $94.5 billion over the FY 2026–2035 budget window.” [25]
  • Because The Congressional Budget Office explains the general risk: “Larger amounts of debt make the United States’ fiscal position more vulnerable to an increase in interest rates.” [46]
  • Because It also warns that “Lawmakers might feel constrained from using federal tax and spending policies to respond to unforeseen events or for other purposes, such as to promote economic activity or strengthen national defense.” [46]
  • So S.2 adds borrowing and interest costs to the financial pressures facing future defense and emergency decisions. Increasing that burden weakens the financial resilience needed for a state that can protect its citizens.
original.con_html:
Response The PRO moves from fiscal cost and sensitivity to interest rates to weaker national readiness without establishing that last step.

  • Because The estimate puts borrowing and interest costs at “$94.5 billion over the FY 2026–2035 budget window.” [25] That measures added expense over ten years, rather than a loss of protective funding or borrowing options.
  • Because The Congressional Budget Office describes greater sensitivity to interest rates: “Larger amounts of debt make the United States’ fiscal position more vulnerable to an increase in interest rates.” [46] Its readiness warning depends on future decisions: “The size of the debt might make lawmakers feel constrained from using deficit-financed fiscal policy to respond to unforeseen events, promote economic activity, or further other goals.” [46]
  • Because Its final S.2 estimate states: “CBO has not reviewed S. 2 for effects on spending subject to appropriation.” [47] That estimate does not assess whether later defense or emergency funding would fall.
  • So The PRO has not shown how the bill’s added costs translate into less room to finance protection, through borrowing limits or changed spending decisions. A budget cost and a general warning about rising national debt do not establish that further effect on readiness.

arguments.title: S.2 pays for drug detection that could help protect the family setting where parents pass on faith.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 6 S.2 pays for drug detection that could help protect the family setting where parents pass on faith.

  • Because Section 103 pays for inspection equipment to combat “the entry or exit of illicit narcotics” [1] and border work for “combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals” [1]. Precursor chemicals are the ingredients used to make drugs.
  • Because The Government Accountability Office (GAO) explains how the equipment works: “These scans produce images that CBP officers review to help detect illegal drugs or other contraband.” [12] CBP is Customs and Border Protection, the federal border agency.
  • Because Southern Baptists also identify a threat to family life: “Opioid abuse destroys the individual user, but it also destroys the family unit by often separating children from their addicted parents” [13]. Opioids include fentanyl.
  • Because Their statement on the family gives parents the job of passing on faith: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values and to lead them, through consistent lifestyle example and loving discipline, to make choices based on biblical truth.” [14]
  • So By addressing opioid abuse that separates children from parents, drug-detection work could help protect the family setting for parents' continuing religious teaching. Passing on faith in this way, and not a general religious support for drug control, is what connects this to Tradition.
arguments.con_html:
Response This argument does not establish its chain from more drug detection to less opioid abuse and protected family teaching.

  • Because Finding drugs does not show a lasting loss of supply. Drug-policy researcher Jonathan Caulkins explains the problem: “There is little point in working hard to seize drugs that can be replaced at a very low cost.” [15]
  • Because GAO also says that the Department of Homeland Security's “ability to fully assess the effectiveness of its efforts is limited.” [16]
  • Because The family practice at the end of the chain is teaching faith: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values” [14].
  • So This argument needs a reason to expect that added detection reduces abuse even though seized drugs can be replaced cheaply. A scanner's ability to reveal hidden items does not supply that step. Without it, this spending is not connected to protecting the family practice of passing on faith.

  • Because The joint Christian report explains the further risk: “In some cases, if the pastor is deported, the congregation may be unable to find a new leader. Similarly, if a substantial portion of the congregation is deported, the church may close.” [18]
  • Because This loss reaches members who remain: “even church members who are citizens or legal permanent residents will be deeply impacted.” [18]
  • So Added removal capacity puts congregations' leaders and members at greater risk. Losing a congregation breaks the continuity of a community that carries Christian teaching, worship and customs. Keeping that community gives [NAME] a reason to oppose S.2.
arguments.con_html:
Response The sources limit how far this warning about closing churches can go.

  • Because The bishop's instruction was a plan to keep leadership: “The bishop has instructed each congregation with endangered pastors to prepare three laypeople to take over, should their leader be deported.” [28]
  • Because The report makes closure depend on more conditions: “In some cases, if the pastor is deported, the congregation may be unable to find a new leader. Similarly, if a substantial portion of the congregation is deported, the church may close.” [18] It says this discussion is “beyond the scope of this report” [18].
  • So The plan to replace leaders answers part of the risk from losing a pastor. The warning about closing is conditional and was not studied in this report. This response does not answer the risk from losing many members.

arguments.title: Added custody puts pastoral care and the Christian duty to visit prisoners at risk.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 5 Added custody puts pastoral care and the Christian duty to visit prisoners at risk.

  • Because Limits on access reached both Protestant and Catholic ministry. Christianity Today reported that Indonesian pastors waited without success to visit a detained member; a Pentecostal pastor also could not enter: “Like the Indonesian pastors, the pastor he met never got in.” [30] Pastoral care means religious care from clergy.
  • Because The problem continued into 2026. An April court order found that a total ban at the Broadview detention center in Illinois “renders plaintiffs’ religious exercise of providing ministry to detainees and migrants effectively impracticable.” [31]
  • Because An April 2026 release from Rep. Jimmy Gomez's office says clergy were denied entry to the Roybal building in Los Angeles on Ash Wednesday and that four were admitted on Good Friday after the office pressed ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement). This shows both a barrier and a fix that needed help from a member of Congress, not a permanent ban at that site. [32]
  • Because The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) defended excluding religious services from field offices: “It is not within standard operating procedure for religious services to be provided in a field office” [33]. The same report describes evidence that people were held in those buildings “for days on end” [33].
  • Note Court relief named particular facilities. The April 7 order required access to “the Broadview facility” [31]; the March 20 order required a process for clergy access to “the Whipple facility” [34], in Minnesota. Those orders did not open every place where added arrests could send Christians.
  • Because Southern Baptist leaders based their appeal on the words of Jesus: “I was in prison and you came to visit me” [24].
  • So Supporting more custody exposes more Christians and their pastors to these barriers. [NAME] has a reason to oppose this risk to prayer, pastoral care and an inherited duty of the church.
arguments.con_html:
Response Documented fixes limit the prediction from earlier bans, while access elsewhere stays uncertain.

  • Because An interim agreement at Broadview led to visits before Congress's June 9 vote: “Faith leaders began daily visits Friday, May 15, 2026” [35]. It allowed spiritual care once a day, including “bringing the Sacraments and other religious items approved beforehand.” [35]
  • Because The April 16 order for the Whipple building stated: “Access is the default.” [36] It required access the same day or a specific, time-limited reason for delay.
  • Because According to the congressional office involved, Roybal gives a third example of both denial and relief: clergy admitted for Good Friday followed a denial on Ash Wednesday and the office's help. One reported visit does not show routine access at Roybal. [32]
  • So Added custody cannot simply be assigned the former bans at sites where access improved. This response is partial: it does not answer added custody at sites without such measures, or where access depends on special help. Neither the reported barriers nor these fixes show one pattern across the country.

arguments.title: Added removals put Christians at risk of religious persecution abroad.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 7 Added removals put Christians at risk of religious persecution abroad.

  • Because This danger has already reached Christian converts. In November 2025, the BBC reported a husband's account: “They deported my wife back to Iran even though she is a Christian” [39]. The BBC reported that she had since “been contacted and summoned by Iranian intelligence.” [39]
  • Because The report explains the religious danger: “Converting from Islam is treated as apostasy, and converts face arrest, interrogation and prison terms.” [39] Apostasy means leaving a religion.
  • Because The risk also reaches relatives who go with a deported family member. The joint Christian report warns that this can mean “abandoning the religious freedom that is guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution but is not respected by all countries.” [18]
  • Because Southern Baptists' 2011 religious liberty resolution affirms the freedom “to worship without harassment or impediment from the state” [40] and calls for prayer for Christians “persecuted, imprisoned, or facing execution for their testimony of faith in Jesus.” [40]
  • So More ability to remove people supports a system that has returned Christians to danger and puts the worship of relatives who go with them at risk. Keeping their freedom to live by their faith gives [NAME] a reason to oppose S.2.
arguments.con_html:
Response The persecution evidence does not connect S.2's transport money to more unsafe returns, because the law and other decisions control where people are sent.

  • Because The BBC reports that Ali's wife was returned to Iran and summoned by Iranian intelligence. Her lawyer said sensitive information about her change of religion and other reasons for asking for protection “was not removed before deportation.” [39] This account concerns how protection, destinations and religious information were handled.
  • Because Existing law bars removal to a country when the official finds this kind of threat, with listed exceptions: “the Attorney General may not remove an alien to a country if the Attorney General decides that the alien's life or freedom would be threatened in that country because of the alien's race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.” [41]
  • Because The family report's warning about relatives depends on the destination: “abandoning the religious freedom that is guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution but is not respected by all countries.” [18] Section 202's transport money does not choose destinations or replace decisions about protection.
  • So More removal money alone does not show more returns to religious persecution, including for relatives who move with a deported family member. This does not show that unsafe returns will not happen; the BBC case shows that one did.

S2_UNN_support_01.support:
Point 1 Better-supported border patrols can reduce pollution of water that wildlife uses.

  • Because The Department of the Interior manages many federal lands. It reported that border staff and equipment reduced damaging traffic: “By deploying personnel, equipment, and infrastructure, CBP operations have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2] CBP is Customs and Border Protection, the federal border agency.
  • Because The Forest Service said that people crossing the border leave trash behind: “Perhaps one of the most well known of the impacts of illegal immigration is the litter left behind” [3].
  • Because This trash can ruin water that wild animals drink: “Water sources near this contamination are often so fouled by pollution that wildlife can no longer use them.” [3]
  • So Section 201 pays for staff, and Section 103 pays for surveillance. Both support patrols like the ones Interior describes. Where added patrols reduce crossings through wild areas, they can reduce this pollution. Protecting water that wildlife uses serves [NAME]'s care for nature.
S2_UNN_support_01.response:
Response These local gains do not show that S.2's added patrols would reduce this traffic instead of moving it somewhere else.

  • Because Interior reported gains in some places: “CBP operations have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2]
  • Because The Forest Service reported that stronger controls beside Coronado National Forest “funneled growing amounts of illegal vehicle and foot traffic through the valleys and mountains of the Forest.” [3] “Funneled” means pushed into one place.
  • So Enforcement can reduce traffic in one place and push it into wild land in another. So one step is missing: that added patrols would reduce the traffic near wildlife water, and not only move it.

S2_UNN_support_02.support:
Point 2 Catching people faster protects habitat from damaging traffic and broken livestock fences.

  • Because Section 103 pays for towers on the southwest and northern borders only if CBP (Customs and Border Protection, the federal border agency) has tested and accepted them “to deliver autonomous capabilities.” [1] “Autonomous” means the system works without constant human control.
  • Because CBP reported that people were caught faster with autonomous towers: “The response time from target identification to suspect apprehension dramatically decreased,” [4]
  • Because The Forest Service reported that “unauthorized trails and roads have been created on the Forest by illegal foot and vehicle traffic.” [3] It said that when these trails spread, this “damages and destroys cactus and other sensitive vegetation; disrupts or prohibits revegetation; disturbs wildlife, their security and travel routes; causes soil compaction and erosion” [3].
  • Because Crossing traffic also broke a fence that protected the habitat (home area) of endangered species. The fence became “ineffective in restricting livestock use” [3]. As a result, “This fence damage has allowed the destruction of endangered species habitat to continue” [3].
  • So Paying for staff and faster detection makes it easier to stop damaging traffic and fence damage. That protects plants, wildlife habitat and soil from destruction, which [NAME] values.
S2_UNN_support_02.response:
Response Catching someone faster does not show that there is less damage to trails, plants or fences.

  • Because The tower report describes a narrower result: “The response time from target identification to suspect apprehension dramatically decreased,” [4]
  • Because The Forest Service reported that stronger controls beside Coronado National Forest “funneled growing amounts of illegal vehicle and foot traffic through the valleys and mountains of the Forest.” [3] “Funneled” means pushed into one place.
  • So Speed of response does not measure total travel through habitat or fence damage avoided. Enforcement can also push traffic into wild areas. So this argument does not connect faster catching to less damaging traffic overall.

strength.html: Surveillance money already in law: The Congressional Research Service (CRS), the research office of Congress, says the 2025 budget law (P.L. 119-21) provides $6.17 billion for inspection and surveillance technology. Sources: [5].

S2_UNN_support_03.support:
Point 3 Stopping unlawful traffic can help protect native plants and animals from harmful species brought in from elsewhere.

  • Because In March 2025, the Department of the Interior described harm from unlawful border activity: “national parks, wildlife refuges and the species they protect are adversely impacted by land degradation and destruction from trail cutting, trash accumulation, invasive species introductions” [6]. “Invasive species” are plants or animals that come from elsewhere and harm local nature.
  • Because Border operations have reduced the activity that carries these risks: “CBP operations have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2] CBP is Customs and Border Protection, the federal border agency.
  • So Added staff and surveillance help stop this traffic. Less unlawful travel through parks and refuges can reduce one way that harmful species spread there. Reducing this spread is a way to protect nature.
S2_UNN_support_03.response:
Response This argument treats immigration enforcement as a way to control invasive species, but does not show how stopping people would keep species out.

  • Because Interior lists “invasive species introductions” [6] among the harms, but it does not explain how these species arrive.
  • Because Seeds can travel on people. The National Park Service explains: “Seeds can readily become lodged in our boots and stuck to our clothing.” [7]
  • So The missing step is keeping species from reaching habitat. A person caught after walking through the land may already have carried the seeds there. The list of harms and the general report of reduced border activity do not show that S.2 would reduce this spread.

S2_UNN_support_04.support:
Point 4 Preventing damaging crossings also addresses one cause of destructive wildfires.

  • Because The Forest Service documented the link: “Large numbers of warming and cooking fires built and abandoned by cross-border violators have caused wildfires that have destroyed valuable natural and cultural resources.” [3] “Cross-border violators” means people crossing the border illegally.
  • Because S.2 supports a way of reducing this activity that has worked in some areas. The Department of the Interior reported that border operations “have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2]
  • So Stopping people before they travel and camp in natural areas makes it easier to prevent these fires. Avoiding fires that destroy nature gives [NAME] another reason to favor S.2.
S2_UNN_support_04.response:
Response The sources do not connect S.2's added arrests to fewer abandoned campfires in these forests.

  • Because The Forest Service names “warming and cooking fires built and abandoned by cross-border violators” [3] as a cause of wildfires.
  • Because The same testimony says that enforcement beside Coronado National Forest “funneled growing amounts of illegal vehicle and foot traffic through the valleys and mountains of the Forest.” [3] “Funneled” means pushed into one place.
  • So This argument relies on Interior's general report of reductions in some areas. But the fire evidence comes from a forest where enforcement pushed traffic into the backcountry (remote land). So added patrols may not mean fewer people camping there. One step is missing: that patrols would reduce crossings in fire-prone wild land, and not only move them.

S2_UNN_support_05.support:
Point 5 Paying for Border Patrol's other duties supports early fire warnings and calls for firefighting help.

  • Because Section 101 pays to “hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and Border Patrol support personnel to conduct functions other than immigration enforcement and customs functions.” [1]
  • Because These agents give fire warnings. In April 2025, agents saw smoke near the border. “They promptly contacted fire crews from the Forest Service and Mexico.” [8]
  • Because U.S. crews put out the small fires that followed: “U.S. fire services swiftly put out spot fires caused by embers that blew across the border, while Mexican crews battled the main blaze to the south.” [8]
  • Because Agents also called for help during a 2021 fire in the Jacumba Wilderness: “El Centro Station notified the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) of the situation.” [9] This response worked: “The combined resources and firefighting efforts were able to control the fires.” [9]
  • So S.2 supports staff who notice fires and bring in the crews needed to control them. This helps protect natural areas from spreading fire.
S2_UNN_support_05.response: No response specific to this point is provided.

S2_UNN_support_06.support:
Point 6 Joint patrols let land officers focus on protecting natural resources.

  • Because The Forest Service reported that border enforcement took its officers away from conservation: “The law enforcement efforts in response to cross-border violators and smugglers of controlled substances diverts our officers from other management and resource protection activities.” [3]
  • Because The Department of the Interior described “intelligence-supported joint patrols on Interior and USFS managed lands.” [2] (Joint patrols use officers from more than one agency. USFS is the Forest Service.) Interior reported that duties were divided: “Interior law enforcement officers focused on resource mission-related violations during this operation.” [2] These are violations that harm the land and its resources.
  • Because Together with the immigration staff in Section 201, Section 103 pays for “Enhancing border security by combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals, at the southwest, northern, and maritime borders.” [1]
  • So S.2 supports the border-enforcement side of this division of work. Keeping land officers' time for protecting natural resources serves [NAME]'s care for nature.
S2_UNN_support_06.response:
Response A division of duties inside a joint patrol does not show that S.2's money protects land officers' time for conservation.

  • Because Interior describes patrols that use officers from both agencies: “Border Patrol agents frequently conduct joint patrols with Interior law enforcement personnel on Interior-managed lands, including national parks, wildlife refuges, and public lands.” [2]
  • Because Its account of one operation says: “Interior law enforcement officers focused on resource mission-related violations during this operation.” [2]
  • So This shows who did what inside joint operations, and those operations also use land officers.
