  • Because Section 202 pays ICE staff, “including officers, agents, investigators, attorneys and support staff, to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” [1] ICE is Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
  • Because Section 203 also allows money “for DHS and State officers to carry out immigration enforcement” [2]. DHS means the Department of Homeland Security.
  • Because The campaign has already moved federal investigators: “The Trump administration has already diverted thousands of law enforcement officials at multiple agencies away from their work tackling serious crime and national security investigations to focus on immigration” [36].

S2_SES_oppose_05.response:
Response This argument does not show that S.2 worsens the staff shortage behind the reported diversion of investigators.

  • Because Section 202 pays for “Hiring, paying, training, and equipping” [1] immigration staff. So more immigration work can use new staff. This is not evidence of more transfers from other cases.

  • Because Within that amount, “$108,500,000 shall be used to hire, pay, and equip additional child exploitation investigators and forensics analysts” [1]. This pays for additional people for the work that this argument says lacks staff.
  • So The protected investigation money matters to the claimed staff loss, even though other money can pay for immigration assignments. This argument has not shown that the new hiring money leaves a larger staff gap or causes more investigators to leave other protective work.

S2_SES_oppose_06.support:

S2_SES_oppose_06.response:
Response The observer example does not show that S.2 expands the monitoring used to discourage people from watching.

  • Because S.2 pays for technology maintenance for “enforcement and removal operations” [1]. Its additional DHS money is also tied to listed uses: “for the purposes provided in this title or in paragraph (3) or (7) of section 100051 of Public Law 119-21.” [1] These spending permissions do not name an added project to track peaceful observers.
  • So This argument does not connect added monitoring from S.2 to more intimidation or less effective watching. A threat that can work without the claimed database does not supply this link.

strength.html: The 2025 budget law provided Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) with $45 billion for detention and $29.85 billion for other functions. A June 9 analysis reports plans to use that money to cover (offset) $416 million in detention costs and $350 million in transport costs in fiscal year 2027. Sources: [5], [30].
The sources do not settle how much S.2 would add. Sources: [5], [30].

The estimate from the American Action Forum is a ten-year cost. The warning from the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) is general and conditional. CBO says it has not reviewed S.2 for effects on spending that Congress decides each year (spending subject to appropriation). These facts matter for how much pressure S.2 adds.

S2_TR_support_06.support:
Point 6 S.2 pays for drug detection that could help protect the family setting where parents pass on faith.

  • Because Section 103 pays for inspection equipment to combat “the entry or exit of illicit narcotics” [1] and border work for “combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals” [1]. Precursor chemicals are the ingredients used to make drugs.
  • Because The Government Accountability Office (GAO) explains how the equipment works: “These scans produce images that CBP officers review to help detect illegal drugs or other contraband.” [12] CBP is Customs and Border Protection, the federal border agency.
  • Because Southern Baptists also identify a threat to family life: “Opioid abuse destroys the individual user, but it also destroys the family unit by often separating children from their addicted parents” [13]. Opioids include fentanyl.
  • Because Their statement on the family gives parents the job of passing on faith: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values and to lead them, through consistent lifestyle example and loving discipline, to make choices based on biblical truth.” [14]
  • So By addressing opioid abuse that separates children from parents, drug-detection work could help protect the family setting for parents' continuing religious teaching. Passing on faith in this way, and not a general religious support for drug control, is what connects this to Tradition.
S2_TR_support_06.response:
Response This argument does not establish its chain from more drug detection to less opioid abuse and protected family teaching.

  • Because Finding drugs does not show a lasting loss of supply. Drug-policy researcher Jonathan Caulkins explains the problem: “There is little point in working hard to seize drugs that can be replaced at a very low cost.” [15]
  • Because GAO also says that the Department of Homeland Security's “ability to fully assess the effectiveness of its efforts is limited.” [16]
  • Because The family practice at the end of the chain is teaching faith: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values” [14].
  • So This argument needs a reason to expect that added detection reduces abuse even though seized drugs can be replaced cheaply. A scanner's ability to reveal hidden items does not supply that step. Without it, this spending is not connected to protecting the family practice of passing on faith.

S2_TR_oppose_01.support:
Point 1 Added removals threaten family unity and parents' passing on of faith.

  • Because A joint evangelical and Catholic report identifies the risk of “marriages being divided or children being raised apart from one or both parents due to deportations” [18].
  • Because Southern Baptists affirm that “God has ordained the family as the foundational institution of human society” [19].
  • Because Their statement of faith, the Baptist Faith and Message, adopted in 2000, ties passing on faith to parents' daily example: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values and to lead them, through consistent lifestyle example and loving discipline, to make choices based on biblical truth.” [20]
  • So More resources for removals (deportations) put Christian families at greater risk of being forced apart.
  • So Living apart disrupts shared family life and parents' daily teaching. Keeping these family duties gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the added money.

Section 202 does not separate removals that would continue anyway from added removals. Sources: [21].
S2_TR_oppose_01.response: No response specific to this point is provided.

strength.html: The director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) said the 2025 budget law provided $15.4 billion for removals. Sources: [21].
These sources do not estimate added removals for Christian families. Sources: [21].

The director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) described about 11,000 new hires under the 2025 budget law. Staff for the minority party on the Senate Budget Committee report that $62 billion of ICE's money from that law was not yet committed to spending (unobligated) at the end of May 2026. The administration calls S.2 funding for 'base operations'. Sources: [21], [22], [23].
The sources do not settle how much S.2 would add. Sources: [21], [22], [23].

S2_TR_oppose_02.support:
Point 2 Added enforcement threatens shared worship, religious teaching and familiar church rites.

  • Because Southern Baptist leaders reported that fear of enforcement left even lawful immigrants “afraid to gather to worship God and receive spiritual care in their local church” [24].
  • Because A June 8, 2026 report quotes an amended church lawsuit that describes a change in religious practice: “Baptisms that previously would have been occasions for communal worship and celebration are now being held in private.” [25] A baptism is a Christian rite of joining the church.
  • Because The Southern Baptists' statement of faith says Sunday “should include exercises of worship and spiritual devotion, both public and private.” [20]
  • Because Their religious liberty commission warned that enforcement at churches would hold back teaching and sharing the faith: “our central mission of Gospel proclamation and biblical formation will be inhibited.” [26]
  • Note A February court order protecting churches covered only properties of the churches in the case, defined as places “regularly used by Plaintiffs to conduct religious services” [27]. It did not protect every church. The June 8 report describes continued fear and disrupted worship despite that order.
  • So Adding resources to enforcement that already keeps people from church puts shared worship, teaching and rites under more pressure. [NAME] has a reason to oppose this threat to practicing and passing on the faith.
S2_TR_oppose_02.response: No response specific to this point is provided.

S2_TR_oppose_03.support:
Point 3 Removing pastors and members threatens the continuity of congregations.

  • Because The risk reaches evangelical church leaders. The Associated Press reported that a bishop had told churches with pastors at risk of deportation “to prepare three laypeople to take over, should their leader be deported.” [28] Laypeople are church members who are not clergy.
  • Because The joint Christian report explains the further risk: “In some cases, if the pastor is deported, the congregation may be unable to find a new leader. Similarly, if a substantial portion of the congregation is deported, the church may close.” [18]
  • Because This loss reaches members who remain: “even church members who are citizens or legal permanent residents will be deeply impacted.” [18]
  • So Added removal capacity puts congregations' leaders and members at greater risk. Losing a congregation breaks the continuity of a community that carries Christian teaching, worship and customs. Keeping that community gives [NAME] a reason to oppose S.2.
S2_TR_oppose_03.response:
Response The sources limit how far this warning about closing churches can go.

  • Because The bishop's instruction was a plan to keep leadership: “The bishop has instructed each congregation with endangered pastors to prepare three laypeople to take over, should their leader be deported.” [28]
  • Because The report makes closure depend on more conditions: “In some cases, if the pastor is deported, the congregation may be unable to find a new leader. Similarly, if a substantial portion of the congregation is deported, the church may close.” [18] It says this discussion is “beyond the scope of this report” [18].
  • So The plan to replace leaders answers part of the risk from losing a pastor. The warning about closing is conditional and was not studied in this report. This response does not answer the risk from losing many members.

S2_TR_oppose_04.support:
Point 4 Added enforcement can interrupt an established church food ministry.

  • Because Church leaders said that a January 2026 Border Patrol arrest on church grounds stopped their aid work. KTLA reported: “The raid interrupted the church’s food distribution ministry and an event for mothers and children in the church garden.” [29] A ministry is religious service work by a church.
  • Because The 2018 Southern Baptist immigration resolution teaches that “Scripture is clear on the believer’s hospitality towards immigrants” [19] and urges pastors “to exhort their congregations to serve their local immigrant communities” [19].
  • So More resources for operations that have interrupted this church's ministry raise the risk of more interruptions to its continuing shared religious work. Keeping this established ministry, and not a general support for helping strangers, is what gives [NAME] a Tradition reason.
S2_TR_oppose_04.response: No response specific to this point is provided.

S2_TR_oppose_05.support:
Point 5 Added custody puts pastoral care and the Christian duty to visit prisoners at risk.

  • Because Limits on access reached both Protestant and Catholic ministry. Christianity Today reported that Indonesian pastors waited without success to visit a detained member; a Pentecostal pastor also could not enter: “Like the Indonesian pastors, the pastor he met never got in.” [30] Pastoral care means religious care from clergy.
  • Because The problem continued into 2026. An April court order found that a total ban at the Broadview detention center in Illinois “renders plaintiffs’ religious exercise of providing ministry to detainees and migrants effectively impracticable.” [31]
  • Because An April 2026 release from Rep. Jimmy Gomez's office says clergy were denied entry to the Roybal building in Los Angeles on Ash Wednesday and that four were admitted on Good Friday after the office pressed ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement). This shows both a barrier and a fix that needed help from a member of Congress, not a permanent ban at that site. [32]
  • Because The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) defended excluding religious services from field offices: “It is not within standard operating procedure for religious services to be provided in a field office” [33]. The same report describes evidence that people were held in those buildings “for days on end” [33].
  • Note Court relief named particular facilities. The April 7 order required access to “the Broadview facility” [31]; the March 20 order required a process for clergy access to “the Whipple facility” [34], in Minnesota. Those orders did not open every place where added arrests could send Christians.
  • Because Southern Baptist leaders based their appeal on the words of Jesus: “I was in prison and you came to visit me” [24].
  • So Supporting more custody exposes more Christians and their pastors to these barriers. [NAME] has a reason to oppose this risk to prayer, pastoral care and an inherited duty of the church.
S2_TR_oppose_05.response:
Response Documented fixes limit the prediction from earlier bans, while access elsewhere stays uncertain.

  • Because An interim agreement at Broadview led to visits before Congress's June 9 vote: “Faith leaders began daily visits Friday, May 15, 2026” [35]. It allowed spiritual care once a day, including “bringing the Sacraments and other religious items approved beforehand.” [35]
  • Because The April 16 order for the Whipple building stated: “Access is the default.” [36] It required access the same day or a specific, time-limited reason for delay.
  • Because According to the congressional office involved, Roybal gives a third example of both denial and relief: clergy admitted for Good Friday followed a denial on Ash Wednesday and the office's help. One reported visit does not show routine access at Roybal. [32]
  • So Added custody cannot simply be assigned the former bans at sites where access improved. This response is partial: it does not answer added custody at sites without such measures, or where access depends on special help. Neither the reported barriers nor these fixes show one pattern across the country.

S2_TR_oppose_07.support:
Point 7 Added removals put Christians at risk of religious persecution abroad.

  • Because This danger has already reached Christian converts. In November 2025, the BBC reported a husband's account: “They deported my wife back to Iran even though she is a Christian” [39]. The BBC reported that she had since “been contacted and summoned by Iranian intelligence.” [39]
  • Because The report explains the religious danger: “Converting from Islam is treated as apostasy, and converts face arrest, interrogation and prison terms.” [39] Apostasy means leaving a religion.
  • Because The risk also reaches relatives who go with a deported family member. The joint Christian report warns that this can mean “abandoning the religious freedom that is guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution but is not respected by all countries.” [18]
  • Because Southern Baptists' 2011 religious liberty resolution affirms the freedom “to worship without harassment or impediment from the state” [40] and calls for prayer for Christians “persecuted, imprisoned, or facing execution for their testimony of faith in Jesus.” [40]
  • So More ability to remove people supports a system that has returned Christians to danger and puts the worship of relatives who go with them at risk. Keeping their freedom to live by their faith gives [NAME] a reason to oppose S.2.
S2_TR_oppose_07.response:
Response The persecution evidence does not connect S.2's transport money to more unsafe returns, because the law and other decisions control where people are sent.

  • Because The BBC reports that Ali's wife was returned to Iran and summoned by Iranian intelligence. Her lawyer said sensitive information about her change of religion and other reasons for asking for protection “was not removed before deportation.” [39] This account concerns how protection, destinations and religious information were handled.
  • Because Existing law bars removal to a country when the official finds this kind of threat, with listed exceptions: “the Attorney General may not remove an alien to a country if the Attorney General decides that the alien's life or freedom would be threatened in that country because of the alien's race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.” [41]
  • Because The family report's warning about relatives depends on the destination: “abandoning the religious freedom that is guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution but is not respected by all countries.” [18] Section 202's transport money does not choose destinations or replace decisions about protection.
  • So More removal money alone does not show more returns to religious persecution, including for relatives who move with a deported family member. This does not show that unsafe returns will not happen; the BBC case shows that one did.

strength.html: The director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) described about 11,000 new hires under the 2025 budget law. Staff for the minority party on the Senate Budget Committee report that $62 billion of ICE's money from that law was not yet committed to spending (unobligated) at the end of May 2026. The administration calls S.2 funding for 'base operations'. Sources: [21], [22], [23].
The sources do not settle how much S.2 would add. Sources: [21], [22], [23].

S2_C01.support: The legal limit keeps this money away from immigration and customs work: it must be used “for functions other than” those missions. [1] HSI has done this other work in the past, including cases about trafficking, fraud and cyberattacks. [18]
S2_C01.response: Senators reported in January 2026 that “entire HSI units have reportedly been reassigned” [21] to immigration enforcement. Cato, a policy institute, reported in September 2025 that HSI “is suspending investigations into human trafficking, child exploitation, cybercrime” [23]. Section 202 separately pays staff in “all its directorates” [1] to do immigration enforcement. So the legal limit controls how this money is spent, but it does not decide where other staff are assigned. These are reports about staff who already worked at HSI. They do not show where Section 102 hires would work, and they do not show that the money cannot reach this work.

S2_C02.support: The Department of the Interior said: “CBP operations have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” [2]

S2_C03.support: Section 103 pays for new equipment “as well as other mission support” [1]. The Government Accountability Office (GAO), a federal audit agency, reported that after new systems were deployed, CBP “has increased its scanning of passenger vehicles from 2 percent in fiscal year 2020 to 8 percent in fiscal year 2024” [4]. So more machines have produced more scans.
S2_C03.response: GAO reported: “Some factors have limited the use of the systems, such as limited staff and system outages.” [4] Officials at four field offices “did not always have sufficient staff to fully use the systems.” [16] The inspector general of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), its internal auditor, found that CBP “did not have a well-defined maintenance and sustainment plan” [15]. These findings concern systems bought before S.2.

S2_C04.support: CBP says: “Seizures remove dangerous drugs from illicit supply chains, keep them out of our communities, and deny TCOs valuable profits.” [10] TCOs are criminal groups that work across countries. Researcher Jonathan Caulkins says seizing fentanyl “is not bad and may induce smugglers to take costly steps to reduce their risk of seizures” [15].
S2_C04.response: Researchers Jonathan Caulkins and Peter Reuter write: “But traffickers can easily replace what is seized.” [7] Caulkins also says synthetic opioids “permit seizures to be replaced in days” [5]. A 2026 review found results in different directions and these were associations, not estimates for S.2. [8] The Government Accountability Office (GAO), a federal audit agency, said DHS’s “ability to fully assess the effectiveness of its efforts is limited.” [16] This does not show that seizures have no benefit.

S2_C05.support: ICE says: “When criminal noncitizens complete their sentences, ICE assumes custody and places them in the appropriate removal proceedings.” [18] ICE gives examples, including a man convicted of “first-degree rape of a child” [9] and a man “convicted for murder in Massachusetts in 2007” [7]. A person in custody cannot attack people in the community.
S2_C05.response: Studies of similar programs did not find less crime. One found that Secure Communities “has had no observable effect on the overall crime rate.” [9] Another found that “The activation of 287(g) jail enforcement agreements and anti-detainer policies had no significant impact on violent victimization risk during the period.” [10] A third, using 2005–2010 data, found “no evidence that these 287(g) arrangements had meaningful crime reduction benefits.” [19] Secure Communities shared local arrest fingerprints with immigration officials. 287(g) agreements let trained local police do some immigration work. These studies cover older programs and broad crime measures, not only people with violent convictions, so they do not settle the question.

S2_C06.support:
Reports before Congress's June 9 vote described changes in how agents made arrests: more targeted arrests and fewer large, visible sweeps. These reports also show limits to the changes. Tom Homan, a top administration official on border policy, said immigration agents would keep arresting people they find during operations if those people are in the country illegally. This includes people with no criminal history who were not the original targets. He said such people are “not off the table” [15], meaning agents can still arrest them. Cristóbal Cavazos, who leads a workers center near Chicago, said he has seen as many as seven agents trying to arrest one person. WBEZ reported that this means “people who weren’t the original targets but are nearby might also get arrested.” [28] Mark Krikorian, who leads a group that advocates for immigration restrictions, said the Trump administration had clearly stepped back from its earlier tactics. He then said: “it’s not clear this means they’re actually stepping back from immigration.” [26] Here “they” means the Trump administration. Human Rights Watch said on June 16 that Congress approved S.2 “without adopting essential oversight and accountability reforms.” [27] Lawmakers and activists had proposed reforms such as requiring warrants from judges and stronger bans on racial profiling.

  • Because Human Rights Watch found federal agents in Los Angeles “detaining people based on their perceived race, ethnicity, or national origin” [19].
S2_C06.response: The Associated Press reported a move “away from aggressive, public-facing tactics toward a quieter approach to enforcement.” [26] CBS reported Homan’s account that “Border Patrol agents have not been making seemingly random immigration stops at parking lots and public places.” [15] CBS also reported on Gregory Bovino, the Border Patrol commander who led the large sweeps, and Alex Pretti, a U.S. citizen killed by federal agents in Minneapolis: “Bovino was relieved of his command following Pretti's killing and retired from Border Patrol in March.” [15] Chicago reporting found “more targeted arrests rather than the large, highly visible sweeps seen last fall.” [28] Part of this evidence is an account by an official. This evidence does not show that these tactics have ended.

S2_C07.support: WIRED reports an FBI bulletin: “Criminals posing as US immigration officers have carried out robberies, kidnappings, and sexual assaults in several states” [35]. The FBI linked the rise in these crimes to the “recent increase in ICE enforcement actions” [35].

S2_C08.support: The Brennan Center writes: “The funding will also allow DHS to continue to build surveillance capabilities that facilitate indiscriminate collection of information about Americans as well as immigrants.” [26] Separately, Section 202 of S.2 funds “information technology maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations” [1].

S2_C09.support: Maryland agencies warned: “Exceeding the capacity of the sewer lines would likely result in sewage backups and overflows” [17]. The city of Social Circle said: “the total additional water demand required for a facility of this scale simply exceeds what the City’s system is capable of providing.” [43] S.2 pays for “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions.” [1]
S2_C09.response: There were limits in place before the comparison date. Social Circle had locked the water meter at the planned detention center. Its city manager said: “The lock is there until ICE indicates how water and sewer will be served without exceeding our limited infrastructure capacity” [45]. A court order stopped work at the Williamsport warehouse “during the pendency of this lawsuit” [19], meaning while the case continues. Maryland said upgrades “must comply with applicable State permitting requirements and be funded by DHS.” [17] S.2 does not itself remove these limits. They could change later.

S2_C10.support: The Center for American Progress reports that “U.S. citizen children have experienced family separation as a result of a parent being detained.” [25] A joint evangelical and Catholic report warns of “marriages being divided or children being raised apart from one or both parents due to deportations” [18].

S2_C11.support: Human Rights Watch documented conditions “including overcrowding, degrading treatment and denial of medical care” [19].

S2_C12.support: The Infectious Diseases Society of America warns that fear of seeking care “threatens the health of entire communities, including by delaying the timely identification and treatment of infectious diseases.” [38] KFF, a health research group, reports that “14% of immigrant adults overall say they or a family member have avoided seeking medical care since January 2025 due to immigration-related concerns.” [39] In a 2026 survey in Minneapolis and St. Paul, some adults reported missing appointments or vaccinations because of enforcement concerns. [42]

S2_C13.support: The source says “significant job losses among immigrant workers could mean less demand for other work done by U.S.-born workers.” [29] It also says: “Crackdowns on immigration are harmful to U.S. workers and contractionary for the overall U.S. economy as the labor market weakens and slower population growth drags down demand and public finances.” [40] “Contractionary” means making the economy smaller.

S2_C14.support: The bill’s money is available “until September 30, 2029” [1]. The American Action Forum says S.2 “provides funding for federal agencies that are typically funded through the annual appropriations process.” [25]

S2_C16.support: CBP reported that aircrews treated a man who was “severely dehydrated and suffering from heat exhaustion.” [11] A report describes a boat crew: “Agents rescued that person, observed signs of hypothermia, and provided medical attention.” [23] CBP says its helicopters include “essential aerial relocation, transport, tactical response, rescue, and investigative surveillance functions” [10].

S2_C17.support: ICE lists the models. “The Jail Enforcement Model allows your officers to identify and process removable aliens who have pending or active criminal charges.” [12] “The Task Force Model allows your officers to enforce limited immigration authority while performing routine police duties or as an active participant in an ICE-led task force.” [12] “The Warrant Service Officer allows your officers to serve and execute administrative warrants on aliens in your custody.” [12] One source says the task force model is “currently the most common 287(g) program model” [29].

S2_C18.support: Section 102 provides money “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” [1].

S2_C19.support: The purpose is “to support the identification and rescue of victims of child sexual exploitation and abuse” [1].

S2_C22.support: The money is “to combat the entry or exit of illicit narcotics at ports of entry and along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders.” [1] It also covers “combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals” [1].

S2_C23.support: It covers “hiring, paying, training, and equipping U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents” [1].

S2_C26.support: The section also covers “fleet maintenance and sustainment” [1] and “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions.” [1]

S2_C29.support: The money may not go to towers that “have not been tested and accepted by U.S. Customs and Border Protection to deliver autonomous capabilities.” [1]

S2_C36.response: The Associated Press reported a move “away from aggressive, public-facing tactics toward a quieter approach to enforcement.” [26] CBS reported Homan’s account that “Border Patrol agents have not been making seemingly random immigration stops at parking lots and public places.” [15] CBS also reported on Gregory Bovino, the Border Patrol commander who led the large sweeps, and Alex Pretti, a U.S. citizen killed by federal agents in Minneapolis: “Bovino was relieved of his command following Pretti's killing and retired from Border Patrol in March.” [15] Chicago reporting found “more targeted arrests rather than the large, highly visible sweeps seen last fall.” [28] Part of this evidence is an account by an official. This evidence does not show that these tactics have ended.

S2_C37.support:
Reports before Congress's June 9 vote described changes in how agents made arrests: more targeted arrests and fewer large, visible sweeps. These reports also show limits to the changes. Tom Homan, a top administration official on border policy, said immigration agents would keep arresting people they find during operations if those people are in the country illegally. This includes people with no criminal history who were not the original targets. He said such people are “not off the table” [15], meaning agents can still arrest them. Cristóbal Cavazos, who leads a workers center near Chicago, said he has seen as many as seven agents trying to arrest one person. WBEZ reported that this means “people who weren’t the original targets but are nearby might also get arrested.” [28] Mark Krikorian, who leads a group that advocates for immigration restrictions, said the Trump administration had clearly stepped back from its earlier tactics. He then said: “it’s not clear this means they’re actually stepping back from immigration.” [26] Here “they” means the Trump administration. ui_copy.strengthGuide: Compare the overall case for each direction. Look at the different consequences in the accepted arguments. Consider all of the effects, not only the strongest one. Do not count headings. If two arguments describe the same consequence, count it once. Good evidence for an effect does not mean that the effect is large. There is no formula to calculate a winner.
